questions.stem: Which practice best reduces bias in a computing innovation?

options.text: Using lossy compression on the data
options.why: That is unrelated.

options.text: Collecting more data from the same source as before
options.why: That repeats the existing bias.

options.text: Testing the innovation with a diverse range of users and data
options.why: Correct. Diverse testing reveals unequal performance.
That makes problems harder to find.

questions.explanation: Diverse testing reveals unequal performance.

questions.stem: A student wants to use a song in an app. The song is published with a Creative Commons license that allows reuse with attribution. What should the student do?

options.text: Avoid the song, because licensed content can never be reused
options.why: The license allows reuse.

options.text: Use the song and credit the creator as the license requires
options.why: Correct. The license grants permission with attribution.

options.text: Pay the creator, because Creative Commons always requires payment
options.why: Many Creative Commons licenses are free.

options.text: Use the song without credit, since it is online
options.why: Online content is still protected.

questions.explanation: The license grants permission with attribution.

questions.stem: Volunteers around the world classify millions of telescope images for an astronomy project. What is this called?

That is two programmers at one computer.

questions.stem: Which is the main benefit of procedural abstraction?

options.why: Procedures do not create parallelism.

questions.explanation: That reduces complexity.

questions.stem: Which protocol is primarily responsible for addressing and routing packets to their destination?

options.why: TCP makes delivery reliable and ordered.
Correct. IP handles addresses and routing.
HTTP requests and sends web pages.
UDP sends data quickly without guarantees.

questions.explanation: IP handles addresses and routing.

questions.stem: Run-length encoding replaces each run of a repeated character with its count followed by the character, so AAAB becomes 3A1B. What is the encoding of `CCWWWWCCCCCCCWWWC`?

options.why: The count comes before the character.
Correct. Each run is replaced by its length and character, in order.
Recount the first run.
Each run is encoded separately, in order; runs are not merged.

questions.explanation: The runs are 2 C, 4 W, 7 C, 3 W, 1 C, so the encoding is 2C4W7C3W1C. It is lossless: the original can be rebuilt exactly.

questions.stem: A social media platform built to help friends share photos is also used to spread false news quickly. This is an example of what?

options.why: That concerns access to technology.
That is a programming error.

options.text: An unintended harmful effect of a computing innovation

That is unrelated.

options.text: The innovation has no harmful effects
options.why: Taxi drivers are harmed.

questions.explanation: Effects of innovations are rarely only good or only bad.

questions.stem: Why is multifactor authentication more secure than a password alone?

options.why: A password is usually one of the factors.

questions.stem: What does a certificate authority do?

options.why: It is a trusted security organization.
That is unrelated.

options.text: Verifies that a website's public key belongs to that website
options.why: Correct. This lets users trust encrypted connections.
That is not its role.

questions.stem: For which of the following values does the expression `(x = y) OR ((x > 5) AND (y > 9))` evaluate to true?

Substituting these values gives false.
Substituting these values gives false.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the 8-bit binary representation of the decimal number 94?

options.why: The bits are in reverse order.
That is 95.
That is 92.

questions.explanation: Subtract the largest powers of 2 that fit: 94 = 64 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2, giving 01011110.

questions.stem: Machine learning finds patterns in medical data that help detect disease early, but the same data could reveal private health details. What does this illustrate?

It can create privacy risks.

options.text: Data analysis can have both beneficial and harmful effects
options.why: Correct. The same innovation can help and harm.

options.text: Medical data cannot be analyzed by computers
options.why: It can.

questions.explanation: The same innovation can help and harm.

questions.stem: A task takes 100 seconds sequentially. A parallel version takes 40 seconds. What is the speedup?

options.why: Times are divided, not added.
That is parallel time divided by sequential time.
Correct. Speedup is sequential time divided by parallel time: 100 ÷ 40.
That is the time saved, not the speedup.

questions.explanation: Speedup is sequential time divided by parallel time: 100 ÷ 40.

questions.stem: Which is an example of the digital divide?

options.text: Students in a rural area cannot complete online homework because they lack reliable Internet access
options.why: Correct. Unequal access to technology is the digital divide.

options.text: A program with a logic error
options.why: That is a bug.

options.text: A website that loads slowly for everyone
options.why: Everyone is affected equally.

options.text: Two apps that use different protocols
options.why: That is not about access.

questions.explanation: Unequal access to technology is the digital divide.

questions.stem: Sound is sampled 44,100 times per second to store it digitally. What is the effect of sampling more often?

options.why: More samples mean more data.
Sampled data is digital.
The number of samples affects quality and size.

options.text: The digital version is a closer approximation of the analog sound, but uses more storage
options.why: Correct. More samples capture more detail at the cost of size.

questions.explanation: More samples capture more detail at the cost of size.

questions.stem: A face recognition system works well for some groups but poorly for others. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The computer's processor is too slow
options.why: Speed does not cause unequal accuracy.
It is not.

options.text: The program has a syntax error
options.why: Syntax errors stop programs from running.

questions.explanation: Unrepresentative data creates biased results.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates distributed computing?

options.text: One laptop running a word processor
options.why: That is a single device.

options.text: A program running one instruction at a time
options.why: That is sequential computing.

options.text: Thousands of volunteers' computers each analyze part of a large scientific data set
options.why: Correct. Multiple devices running one program is distributed computing.

options.text: Compressing a file before emailing it
options.why: That is data compression.

questions.explanation: Multiple devices running one program is distributed computing.

questions.stem:
A robot is on a 6-by-6 grid of squares. Rows are numbered 1 to 6 from top to bottom and columns 1 to 6 from left to right. REPEAT 3 TIMES
```text
{
   MOVE_FORWARD()
   ROTATE_LEFT()
}
```

Where does the robot end, and which way does it face?

options.why: Correct. Trace each move and turn in order.
ROTATE_LEFT turns the robot counterclockwise.
The robot moves forward in each pass.
The robot turns in every pass, including the last.

questions.stem: A hiring algorithm learns from ten years of past hiring decisions in which some groups were rarely hired. What is the risk?

questions.stem: A sorted list contains 505 elements. What is the maximum number of elements that binary search must examine to find a value or determine it is not in the list?

options.why: Correct. Each check halves the remaining elements; about 9 checks reduce 505 to none.
2 to the power 9 is already more than 505.
Binary search halves the remaining range at every step.
That is the worst case for linear search.

questions.explanation: 2^8 = 256 is less than 505 but 2^9 = 512 is not, so at most 9 checks are needed.

questions.stem:
The following code segment is intended to display the sum of the values in `nums`.

```text
FOR EACH n IN nums
{
   total ← 0
   total ← total + n
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed when `nums` is `[7, 2, 2, 9]`, and why?

options.text: 7, because the loop stops after one pass
options.why: FOR EACH visits every element.

options.text: 0, because total is reset after the loop
options.why: The reset happens before the addition in each pass.
total is set back to 0 before each addition.

options.text: 9, because total is reset to 0 on every pass
options.why: Correct. The reset inside the loop discards the earlier values.

questions.explanation: Each pass sets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 9, remains. Moving `total ← 0` before the loop fixes it.

questions.stem: A sorted list contains 100,002 elements. What is the maximum number of elements that binary search must examine to find a value or determine it is not in the list?

options.why: Correct. Each check halves the remaining elements; about 17 checks reduce 100,002 to none.
2 to the power 17 is already more than 100002.
Binary search halves the remaining range at every step.
That is the worst case for linear search.

questions.explanation: 2^16 = 65536 is less than 100002 but 2^17 = 131072 is not, so at most 17 checks are needed.

questions.stem:
Consider the following code segment.

```text
nums ← [1, 20, 12, 10, 2, 16]
evens ← []
FOR EACH n IN nums
{
   IF (n MOD 2 = 0)
   {
      APPEND(evens, n)
   }
}
DISPLAY (LENGTH(evens))
```

What is displayed as a result of running the code segment?

options.why: Correct. Apply the condition to every element of the list.
LENGTH counts elements; it does not add them.
Recheck each element.
Even numbers have remainder 0.

questions.explanation: 5 values are even.

questions.stem:
The following code segment is intended to display the sum of the values in `nums`.

```text
FOR EACH n IN nums
{
   total ← 0
   total ← total + n
}
DISPLAY (total)
```

What is displayed when `nums` is `[7, 20, 7, 18]`, and why?

options.text: 0, because total is reset after the loop
options.why: The reset happens before the addition in each pass.

options.text: 7, because the loop stops after one pass
options.why: FOR EACH visits every element.

options.text: 18, because total is reset to 0 on every pass
options.why: Correct. The reset inside the loop discards the earlier values.
total is set back to 0 before each addition.

questions.explanation: Each pass sets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 18, remains. Moving `total ← 0` before the loop fixes it.

questions.stem: What is the probability that the expression `RANDOM(3, 8) ≥ 4` evaluates to true?

options.why: Correct. The values 4 through 8 (5 of them) out of 6 equally likely values from 3 to 8.
4 itself is included by ≥.
RANDOM includes both 3 and 8, so there are 6 values.
That is the probability of the expression being false.

questions.explanation: RANDOM(3, 8) has 6 equally likely results; 5 of them are at least 4.

questions.stem: A network has computers P, Q, R, S, T, U. The direct connections are: P–R, P–U, Q–R, Q–U, R–T, R–U, S–T, S–U. What is the minimum number of connections that must fail for computer R to be unable to communicate with computer U?

options.why: After that many failures a path still remains.
Correct. Removing 4 well-chosen connections separates R from U; removing fewer always leaves a path.
Some set of 4 connections already disconnects them.
Look for the fewest connections whose failure leaves no path.

questions.explanation: R has 4 connections and U has 4. Checking failures systematically shows that 4 is the fewest that leaves no path between them.

questions.title: Written response 1: program design, function and purpose

parts.prompt: Identify the expected users of the program and describe one way the program's design meets the needs of those users.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a specific group of users.
Describes a design feature and connects it to a need of those users.
rubric.example: The program asks only for simple input (the student enters a score after each practice quiz) and gives a clear result (the program displays how many quizzes met the passing score), which helps them help a student see how many practice quizzes they have passed.

parts.prompt: Describe one input to the program and the output it produces. Explain how the output relates to the program's purpose.

rubric.criterion: Describes an input and the corresponding output.
Explains how the output serves the purpose.
rubric.example: The result shows the user the information they need to help a student see how many practice quizzes they have passed.

parts.prompt: Describe how a programmer could use iterative or incremental development, including testing, while creating this program.

rubric.criterion: Describes building or refining the program in stages.

questions.title: Written response 2: algorithms, testing and abstraction

parts.prompt: (Algorithm development) Explain in detailed steps how the algorithm in `countPassing` uses sequencing, selection and iteration to produce its result.

rubric.example: The FOR EACH loop examines every score in the list.
The IF statement checks whether each score is at least the cutoff, and only then increases the count.

rubric.criterion: Describes how the steps in sequence produce the returned value.
rubric.example: The variables are initialized first, updated inside the loop, and the result is returned after the loop ends. For example, countPassing([88, 46, 49, 59, 80, 50], 65) returns 2.

parts.prompt: (Errors and testing) Describe a call to `countPassing` that tests a different condition than `countPassing([88, 46, 49, 59, 80, 50], 65)`. Identify the result the call should produce and explain why that test is useful.

rubric.criterion: Gives a specific call with different arguments.

rubric.example: 1, because 65 meets the cutoff (≥) and 64 does not

rubric.criterion: Explains what condition the test checks.
rubric.example: It checks a boundary or special case that a typical input does not, which could reveal an error the first test would miss.

parts.prompt: (Data and procedural abstraction) Explain how the list `scores` manages complexity in the program. Then explain how the parameters of `countPassing` make the procedure more useful.

rubric.criterion: Explains how the list manages complexity.
rubric.example: Without the list, each score would need its own variable, the number of quizzes would be fixed, and the count would need a separate IF statement per score.

rubric.criterion: Explains how parameters generalize the procedure.
rubric.example: Because the list and the threshold are parameters, the same procedure works for any data and setting, so it can be reused without copying code. To count failing quizzes instead, change the condition to s < cutoff.
